title: Degraded streaming sessions: customer advisory and next steps
content:
Purpose:

This draft is a customer-facing advisory and series of status-page updates for a regression that caused degraded streaming responses (long-tail token buffering and intermittent stalls) observed across multiple regions on 2028-04-10. Use this as the basis for status.redwood.ai updates and partner/enterprise emails.

Summary (short):
- Impact: Intermittent delays in streamed token delivery for real-time/chat-style endpoints. Customers experienced slower token-by-token streaming and occasional multi-second stalls for in-progress responses. No data loss or request body corruption observed.
- Affected surface: streaming endpoints (stream=true) across some autoscaled pools; primarily noticeable on long-lived sessions and large context lengths.
- Current status: mitigations applied 2028-04-10 17:40 PT; most customers are back to normal streaming performance. We are continuing post-incident validation and rolling a permanent fix.

Audience notes:
- This draft is written for engineering contacts, SREs, partner technical leads, and customer success managers handling escalations. Tone should be factual, concise, and include explicit timelines and clear next steps customers can take.

Suggested status page entries (short, timestamped):
1) 2028-04-10 09:12 PT — Identified: Users reporting increased latency and token buffering in streaming responses. Engineers triaging.
2) 2028-04-10 11:05 PT — Investigating: Initial signal points to unusual cache-miss patterns and increased CPU scheduling on streaming workers. Scoped to subset of autoscaled pools in us-west-2 and eu-central-1.
3) 2028-04-10 15:30 PT — Mitigations in progress: Rolled back recent KV-cache eviction tuning to previous TTL; enabled per-session sticky routing for streaming to prevent cross-host reattachment.
4) 2028-04-10 17:40 PT — Partial resolution: Majority of streaming sessions returned to normal token-throughput. Continuing monitoring and validation work.
5) 2028-04-11 10:00 PT — Post-mitigation: Monitoring looks stable; permanent fix scheduled and will be deployed after additional load-testing.

Incident timeline (detailed):
- 2028-04-10 08:54 PT — First customer report via support portal: multi-second stalls while streaming long responses (~>1200 tokens).
- 2028-04-10 09:12 PT — CS triage and escalation to SRE/Serving Runtime.
- 2028-04-10 10:02 PT — Observability team detects increased KV cache miss rate (prefix/KV cache) and elevated context switch rates on streaming workers.
- 2028-04-10 11:05 PT — Repro locally with long-lived streaming session simulator: frequent rehydration of KV cache causing blocking disk reads under certain workloads; worker orchestration created cross-host session handoffs.
- 2028-04-10 13:00 PT — Hypothesis: Recent eviction TTL change (serving-runtime v1.24.0 config) reduced KV cache residency for long contexts; combined with a scheduling race in the streaming manager produced backpressure.
- 2028-04-10 14:10 PT — Runbook actions: increase autoscaler headroom for streaming pools, route new sessions to warm capacity, and temporarily disable the new eviction tuning.
- 2028-04-10 15:30 PT — Rollback of eviction tuning released to affected pools; sticky routing enabled.
- 2028-04-10 17:40 PT — Monitoring shows token streaming p95/p99 returned to baseline; customer reports of stalls drop significantly.
- 2028-04-11 09:00 PT — Begin validation testing under sustained load and mixed long/short sessions.

Root cause (short):
An unintended interaction between a recently deployed KV cache eviction tuning (introduced in serving-runtime v1.24.0) and the streaming session handoff path led to frequent cache misses and unexpected blocking rehydration of KV prefix data. This, combined with a scheduling race in the streaming manager, produced head-of-line blocking for in-flight streams and increased CPU contention on streaming workers.

Root cause (detailed):
- The eviction tuning reduced per-key residency time to optimize memory usage for short bursts. This change worked well for short-lived request patterns but did not account for long-running streaming contexts.
- When a long streaming session crossed a rebalancing boundary (autoscaler or instance restart), the session handoff path attempted to reattach and rehydrate KV cache on the target worker. With the shorter TTL the required KV pages were missing and triggered synchronous disk-backed rehydration under the request critical path.
- The synchronous rehydration code path used a mutex that briefly blocked the streaming IO thread, causing token emission stalls. Under sustained traffic the blocking amplified due to CPU scheduling and kernel preemption interactions.

Customer impact details:
- Observable effect: tokens batched and delivered in bursts, multi-second stalls in otherwise streaming responses, and higher p99 streaming latency.
- Functional impact: responses eventually completed; model outputs were correct (no data corruption). Some real-time experiences (chat UIs, voice assistants) were degraded.
- Scope: ~3–7% of streaming sessions across affected pools during the peak window. Larger context sessions (>1k tokens) and sessions that spanned autoscaler events were disproportionately affected.

Immediate mitigations applied:
1) Rollback: revert KV eviction tuning to prior TTL values in affected autoscaled pools (fast rollback).
2) Sticky routing: enable per-session host affinity for streaming sessions to avoid handoffs mid-response.
3) Autoscaler headroom: increase warm pool sizes for streaming-enabled capacity to reduce churn during traffic spikes.
4) Circuit breaker: introduced a short-circuit that detects synchronous cache rehydration and offloads rehydration to background loader to keep streaming IO hot.

Permanent remediation (planned):
- Code fix in serving-runtime to make KV rehydration asynchronous and lock-free for the streaming hot path (PR referenced in linked_artifacts).
- Add canary tests that simulate long-lived streaming sessions through autoscaler events.
- Restore conservative TTL for long-context workloads while we instrument per-workload residency metrics.
- Improve observability: new metrics for per-session rehydration latency and a streaming-specific SLO dashboard.

What customers can do (actionable):
- If you see issues and can tolerate non-streaming responses temporarily, set streaming=false on affected routes until we confirm the permanent fix; this returns responses in a single chunk and avoids token-by-token stalls.
- For critical real-time workflows, consider using dedicated or reserved capacity pools (Redwood Dedicated) where we can pin warm hosts and avoid autoscaler churn. If you'd like assistance with a temporary Dedicated trial for verification, respond to your CSM or open a support request.
- Implement client-side minimal retry: if streaming stalls longer than X seconds, reissue the request with a session id; we are collecting guidance and sample client patterns for each SDK; see linked_artifacts for SDK PRs.

Communication & next steps:
- Customer success will proactively reach out to top-50 impacted accounts with tailored technical notes and suggested temporary mitigations.
- Engineering will deploy the asynchronous rehydration fix to a canary pool and run a 48-hour sustained mixed-workload test before ramping to all regions. Target permanent rollout: 2028-04-17 (subject to validation).
- We will publish a final post-incident summary (customer-friendly) once the permanent fix is validated; expected by 2028-04-18.

Suggested enterprise email body (concise):
Subject: Update — streaming latency degradation (April 10)
Hello [Customer],
On April 10 we observed intermittent stalls in token-by-token streaming for some sessions. We identified a cache tuning change that reduced residency for long contexts and caused blocking rehydration under certain handoffs. We rolled back the tuning and enabled sticky routing; streaming performance has returned to baseline for most customers. We are deploying a permanent fix that makes cache rehydration asynchronous and will notify you once validated. If you rely on sustained real-time streaming, our team can help accelerate a dedicated capacity trial.
We apologize for the disruption and are available for a technical sync.
Regards,
Aisha Patel — Customer Success Lead

Contact & escalation:
- Primary incident Slack channel: #inc-kv-cache (internal).
- Support escalation: support@redwood.ai (use priority code: STREAM-URGENT).
- CS contacts: Priya Desai (priya@redwood.ai), Jonah Kim (jonah@redwood.ai).

Notes to internal readers:
- Be explicit when referencing rollback: include config delta and affected pools (we have a diff in the linked PR).
- Coordinate all customer emails through CS leads to prevent duplicate outreach.
- Track follow-ups in JIRA-INC-1327 and update the Confluence incident document with postmortem artifacts and graphs.

Draft sign-offs required: eng-serving-runtime, eng-sre, customer-success, communications.

Attachments (for CS use):
- A short FAQ (two-pager) for customer-facing staff explaining why streaming stalls occurred and product-side mitigations (to be attached to the support ticket).
- A one-line status snippet for customer portals: ‘We experienced intermittent streaming token delays on Apr 10; mitigations applied and performance restored. Full details forthcoming.’

End of draft.
